speaker: randwallis
text: Good morning and welcome to an oral argument session for the 5th District Court of Appeal. My name is Rand Wallace. I'll be presiding over this case today and over this panel. We have joining us also from the 5th District, Judge Meredith Sasso, and we also have from the 7th Circuit, Judge Michael Orfinger, who's helping us out today. I want to thank Judge Orfinger for being a part of this panel today. The last case we have on the docket today is Maria, and I would totally butcher the name, so I'm not going to even attempt to say the name, and Mr. Greenlee, I'll have you pronounce it for us, and then versus Federal National Mortgage, and I think it's Mr. Ledeen. speaker: andrewgreenlee
text: Good morning, Your Honors, and may it please the Court. For sake of simplicity, we will refer to the appellant as Miss Poche. I would like to reserve five minutes for rebuttal, if it pleases the Court. Your Honors, the only issue before the Court is whether the original party plaintiff, Aurora Loan Services, had standing at the outset of the case. We would submit that they failed to carry their burden that Aurora had standing. Under the UCC, three classes of parties are entitled to enforce a negotiable instrument. The second is the non-holder in possession of the instrument with the rights of the holder, and the third, in the case of a lost note, is the party that lost the note but is nevertheless entitled to enforce it. In the complaint, the plaintiff alleged it had standing by way of the first method as the holder, but that theory fails as a matter of law. There was no blank endorsement on the note, on the copy of the note that was filed with the Court at the outset. Aurora was not the original lender, and there was no evidence at trial that would establish when the endorsement appeared on the note. So Fannie Mae failed to carry its burden of showing that it was that Aurora was the holder of the note. And it's also worth noting that Fannie Mae didn't even brief the issue on appeal, so we would submit that they abandoned that theory on

speaker: orfinger
text: appeal. There was no lost note. They did say that at the inception, Aurora said that it was, it did say the holder, but it also said it was the servicer, and that Fannie Mae was the owner. It doesn't sound like anyone ever tried to proceed under the theory that Aurora was actually the holder. It seems like they tried to proceed on the theory of of a party in possession with the rights to enforce the note, because they said right out of the box that Fannie Mae was the owner, and that they were the servicer. They did say they were the

speaker: meredithsasso

speaker: andrewgreenlee

speaker: orfinger

speaker: andrewgreenlee
text: Well, I don't think the court has to put blinders on, but I do think that, and this is something that we addressed in our reply brief, that under the principle of party presentation, the court is bound by the case presented by the parties. First, I would submit that the term nonholder in possession with the rights of a holder is not a catch-all phrase. It typically denotes equitable ownership as evidenced by a chain of transfer from one party to the next, all the way down until you get to the party that's bringing suit. I think typically when these cases come before the court and the servicer is bringing the case on behalf of the other party, that party is typically the note holder. There is a long, long line of cases that says that where there is an undated endorsement in blank, we can't presume that it was — that that was a condition of the note at the time it was filed. So I think that if the court were to hold otherwise, it would fly in the face of many, many, many, many cases.

text: We don't dispute that as a general proposition. We think that there are — well, our first argument is that they never pled that we're the nonholder in possession with the rights of a holder. text: Yeah. Thank you, Your Honor. I am glad to address that point. speaker: orfinger

speaker: andrewgreenlee
text: I don't believe — I think the defendant was the proponent of that piece of evidence. The defendant was trying to introduce that into — I didn't — when I reviewed the trial transcript, I didn't see that the defendant — there was many objections based on hearsay at trial, but I don't think to this particular document, particularly since the defendant was the proponent of this document, that hearsay wasn't an objection that was lodged by the plaintiff or the defendant. And if I'm wrong on that, I apologize, but I didn't catch that in my review of the trial transcript. One final point regarding the standard of review. It is true that if there is competent substantial evidence, that the judgment should be affirmed. We agree with that as a legal proposition. We just don't think that there was any competent substantial evidence that suffices under the existing case law that would satisfy the allegations in the complaint that they were the holder of the note. That is a term of legal significance. Ms. Poche had every right to rely on that when she proceeded to trial, and she disproved that theory at trial under longstanding precedent, you know, an undated blank endorsement. If it's not consistent with the copy of the note filed at trial, it's insufficient to establish that they had standing at the outset of the case. And with regard to the unpled theory that they were the servicer, and therefore they had standing as a servicer, as an initial matter, there is no — the statute doesn't say, well, there's a fourth way that you can prove standing, and it's as a servicer. I think if you are proving standing as a servicer, it still has to be kind of as a derivative standing from one of the three statutorily recognized forms of standing that are codified in the statute. And we don't believe that they proved the only method of standing that they alleged. And so we would ask the court to reverse the entry of final judgment and remand for the entry of an order involuntarily dismissing this action.

speaker: randwallis
